flow.title: Meet comments
flow.body:
A comment is a note for people reading the code. Python ignores it when the program runs.

Start a one-line comment with `#`:

`# Save the player's score`

A useful comment explains purpose. It should not repeat every obvious line.

avatar.text: Let us look at meet comments together. A comment is a note for people reading the code. Python ignores it when the program runs. Everything after it on that line is skipped by Python, but it can help you, a teacher, or a teammate understand the reason for the code. Do not rush to memorise every symbol. lessons.goal: Choose readable variable names and follow simple Python naming rules.

flow.title: Names should show meaning
flow.body:
A good variable name tells the reader what the value means.

Use lowercase words joined with underscores:

`player_score = 20`

A name cannot begin with a number, contain spaces, or use a Python keyword such as `if`.

avatar.text: Let us look at names should show meaning together. A good variable name tells the reader what the value means. Use lowercase words joined with underscores: `player_score = 20` A name cannot begin with a number, contain spaces, or use a Python keyword such as `if`. Python programmers often call this style snake_case. Clear names reduce guessing and make mistakes easier to spot. Do not rush to memorise every symbol. Follow the idea from left to right, and use the example on the screen as your guide.

flow.title: What type is this value?
flow.body:
The `type()` function reports the kind of value Python is using.

`type('hello')` gives `str`.

`type(5)` gives `int`.

`type(2.5)` gives `float`.

flow.title: Type conversion
flow.body:
Conversion changes a value from one type to another.

`int('12')` makes the integer `12`.

`float('3.5')` makes the decimal `3.5`.

`str(8)` makes the text `'8'`.

Only convert values that make sense. `int('cat')` causes an error.

avatar.text: Let us look at type conversion together. Only convert values that make sense. `int('cat')` causes an error. Conversion is useful when you need to calculate with input or combine a number with text. First check what the value contains, then choose the correct conversion. Do not rush to memorise every symbol. Follow the idea from left to right, and use the example on the screen as your guide.

lessons.title: elif: More Than Two Choices
lessons.goal: Use elif to check another condition when the first condition is false.

avatar.text: Welcome to Better Decisions and Lists! You completed Clearer Code—well done. Sometimes a program needs small, medium, or large instead of only yes or no.

flow.title: A chain of choices
flow.body:
`if` checks the first condition. `elif` means “else if” and checks another condition. `else` handles anything left.

Python checks from top to bottom. The first true branch runs.

avatar.text: Let us look at a chain of choices together. `if` checks the first condition. `elif` means “else if” and checks another condition. `else` handles anything left. Python checks from top to bottom. The first true branch runs. Order matters. Put the conditions in a sensible order so an early branch does not catch a value before the correct branch is reached. Do not rush to memorise every symbol. Follow the idea from left to right, and use the example on the screen as your guide.

question.question: What does elif mean?
question.explanation: elif checks another condition after an earlier condition is false.

flow.title: Let us read the example together
flow.body:
Here is the example we are about to run:

```python
score = 7
if score >= 10:
    print('Gold')
elif score >= 5:
    print('Silver')
else:
    print('Keep trying')
```

What to notice:

- The first condition is false.
- The elif condition is true, so Python prints Silver and skips the else branch.
- Step by step: First, type `score = 7`.
- Next, type `if score >= 10:`.

avatar.text: Now let us connect the idea to the code before it runs. The first condition is false. The elif condition is true, so Python prints Silver and skips the else branch. Step by step: First, type `score = 7`. Next, type `if score >= 10:`. Then, indent the line and type `print('Gold')` so it belongs to the block above it. After that, type `elif score >= 5:`. Finally, indent the line and type `print('Silver')` so it belongs to the block above it. A single equals sign stores a value under a name. A colon opens a block, and the lines inside that block must be indented. Quotation marks show text values. Watch the code appear from top to bottom. After it runs, compare the output with what each line was expected to do.

flow.title: Logical operators
flow.body:

flow.title: Changing a list
flow.body:
`append()` adds an item to the end.

`insert()` adds an item at a chosen position.

`remove()` removes a matching value.

`pop()` removes an item and can return it.
